name: Olaplex bond builder

card.summary: Brand-defining bond-repair hair treatment; widely sold, but only company-cited testing and a lawsuit history in the sources.
card.aka: Olaplex No.3, bond builders, bond-repair treatments
card.note: 2023 lawsuits allege hair damage and loss; the company disputes them.

quick.overview:
Olaplex is a hair-care brand that popularized bond-repair treatments, which are applied during or after bleaching and coloring to protect hair. Its patented active ingredient is bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate.

The company cites third-party testing and a 2024 review of the ingredient; the sources reviewed contain no independent clinical trials.
quick.mechanism: The stated mechanism is that the ingredient binds keratin and reconnects broken disulfide bonds within the hair, which chemical services and heat can sever.
quick.risks: A 2023 lawsuit by 28 women alleged hair damage and hair loss, and that older Lilial-containing formulas stayed on sale. Olaplex disputes the claims and cites third-party safety testing; a judge declined class treatment. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by regulators like the US FDA.

lead: Olaplex is an American hair-care brand founded in 2014 whose products are marketed as rebuilding hair damaged by chemical, thermal and mechanical stress [1][2]. Its products contain a patented ingredient, bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate, which the company says reconnects broken disulfide bonds in hair [1][2]. People use bond-building treatments to keep bleached, coloured or heat-styled hair stronger, smoother and less prone to breaking, so they can maintain lighter or styled looks.

The brand launched as a salon-only treatment used during bleaching and colouring, then added retail products such as the No.3 treatment, No.4 shampoo and No.5 conditioner, creating the broader category of bond-repair or bond-building treatments [2]. Wikipedia summarises a July 2024 review of the ingredient (by Pattiwar and colleagues) as describing how it reacts with cysteine residues in keratin to restore disulfide bonds and form a protective barrier, with effects most noticeable on thick, curly, fine or damaged hair and less evident on healthy hair [1].

Olaplex has also been the subject of litigation, including a trade-secret dispute with L'Oreal and a 2023 lawsuit by women alleging hair damage and hair loss, which the company disputes [1]. No independent clinical trial of Olaplex itself was found.

chain: Ingredient reacts with keratin in damaged hair
Broken disulfide bonds are reconnected (as described)
Hair is stronger and smoother after bleaching, colour or heat
angle.text: Bond builders are used during and after lightening, colouring or heat styling to keep hair from feeling brittle and breaking. Users and stylists report smoother, stronger-feeling hair; the effect is described as most noticeable on damaged hair.

infobox: Dean Christal; developed with chemists Craig Hawker and Eric Pressly [1][2]
Advent International (2019); Nasdaq listing 2021; Henkel acquisition 2026 [1]

paras: Hair strength and shape depend partly on disulfide bonds between keratin chains, which bleaching, colouring and chemical services can break. Olaplex's stated approach is to bind to and rebuild these links during and after such services [2]. Product lines include a salon bond-building step, shampoos, conditioners and styling products, and in 2024 the brand introduced bond-shaping technology aimed at curl definition [2].
Wikipedia states the brand advertises that it rebuilds broken bonds caused by chemical, thermal and mechanical damage [1].

According to Grokipedia, the technology was developed in the early 2010s by UC Santa Barbara chemist Craig Hawker and former student Eric Pressly, and the first patent was filed in 2014. Dean Christal built the company around professional salon distribution [2]. Advent International acquired Olaplex in 2019, and the company listed on Nasdaq on September 30, 2021, raising about 1.5 billion US dollars [1].

Around 2015 Olaplex and L'Oreal discussed a possible takeover that did not proceed; Olaplex later sued over trade secrets, a jury found L'Oreal liable in 2019, the verdict was overturned on appeal, and the companies settled [1]. In 2026 Henkel acquired the company for about 1.4 billion dollars [1].

In February 2023, 28 women sued Olaplex alleging that its products damaged hair and caused hair loss, and that older formulas containing Lilial, a chemical considered potentially toxic to reproduction, remained on sale after its removal [1]. Olaplex responded with third-party testing that it says shows its products are safe. By June 2023 a proposed class action had over 100 plaintiffs, and a federal judge found the claims too varied for class treatment [1]. Wikipedia reports that the lawsuits affected hairstylist endorsements and sales, and that the share price fell about 89 percent by the end of 2023 [1].

A 2025 Pharmaceuticals paper reported three new thiol-reactive cross-linking agents tested on human hair fibres, with the best performer giving the largest gains in tensile strength and elasticity and re-forming disulfide bonds in cysteine reactivity tests. The abstract does not name Olaplex or its ingredient, but describes the same general approach of chemically regenerating disulfide bridges in damaged hair [3].

No studies found testing Olaplex products in people. The research referenced is the 2024 ingredient review summarised by Wikipedia, the company's own third-party safety testing, and laboratory work on related disulfide cross-linking agents [1][3].

timeline.event: Olaplex founded and first patent filed [1][2].
Advent International acquires Olaplex; L'Oreal trade-secret jury verdict later overturned on appeal [1].
Initial public offering on Nasdaq on September 30 [1].
Lawsuit by 28 women alleging hair damage; later proposed class action [1].
Bond-shaping technology for curls introduced; ingredient review published [1][2].
